questions.question_text: Identify any outliers in the dataset $2, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 40, 46$ using the formal $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule.

options.why: Used $Q_3 + \text{IQR} = 30 + 12 = 42$ instead of the upper fence of $48$, incorrectly classifying $46$ as an outlier.
Used $Q_1 - \text{IQR} = 18 - 12 = 6$ instead of the lower fence of $0$, incorrectly classifying $2$ as an outlier.
Used $1 \times \text{IQR}$ instead of $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$, giving incorrect fences of $18 - 12 = 6$ and $30 + 12 = 42$, which flag only $2$ and $46$.

questions.solution_text:
$Q_1 = 18, Q_3 = 30$
$\text{IQR} = 30 - 18 = 12$
$\text{Lower fence} = 18 - 1.5 \times 12 = 0$
$\text{Upper fence} = 30 + 1.5 \times 12 = 48$
All values lie between $0$ and $48$, so there are no outliers.

questions.question_text: Identify any outliers in the dataset $4, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 32, 34, 36, 40, 52$ using the formal $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule.

options.why: Reversed the comparison directions, testing whether the minimum exceeds the lower fence of $6$ and whether the maximum is below the upper fence of $54$.
Used $1 \times \text{IQR}$ instead of $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$, giving incorrect fences of $24 - 12 = 12$ and $36 + 12 = 48$.
Subtracted $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ from the IQR instead of $Q_1$, obtaining an incorrect lower fence of $12 - 18 = -6$.

questions.solution_text:
$Q_1 = 24, Q_3 = 36$
$\text{IQR} = 36 - 24 = 12$
$\text{Lower fence} = 24 - 1.5 \times 12 = 6$
$\text{Upper fence} = 36 + 1.5 \times 12 = 54$
Since $4 < 6$, $4$ is an outlier. All other values lie within the fences.

questions.question_text:
The five-number summary for a dataset is $\text{Min} = 4, Q_1 = 15, Q_2 = 22, Q_3 = 31, \text{Max} = 58$.
Using the formal $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule, which of the following is true?

options.text: $58$ is an outlier because it is greater than the upper fence of $55$.
$4$ is an outlier because it is less than the lower fence of $5$.
options.why: Calculated $1.5 \times 16$ as $10$, giving the incorrect lower fence $15 - 10 = 5$; the correct lower fence is $15 - 24 = -9$.
Assumed both extreme values are outliers without evaluating the lower fence correctly.

options.text: There are no outliers in this dataset.
options.why: Failed to compare the maximum of $58$ against the upper fence of $55$.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{IQR} = 31 - 15 = 16$
$\text{Lower fence} = 15 - 1.5 \times 16 = -9$
$\text{Upper fence} = 31 + 1.5 \times 16 = 55$
Since $58 > 55$, $58$ is an outlier.
Since $4 \ge -9$, $4$ is not an outlier.

questions.question_text:
A set of $10$ scores is: $2, 20, 21, 23, 25, 26, 28, 30, 32, 35$.
Given $Q_1 = 21$ and $Q_3 = 30$, determine which value, if any, is an outlier.

options.why: Incorrectly tested only the maximum against $Q_3 = 30$, classifying $35 > 30$ as an outlier and failing to test $2$ against the lower fence.
Assumed both the minimum and maximum must be outliers.
Did not calculate the lower fence of $7.5$ to test the minimum score of $2$.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{IQR} = 30 - 21 = 9$
$\text{Lower fence} = 21 - 1.5 \times 9 = 7.5$
$\text{Upper fence} = 30 + 1.5 \times 9 = 43.5$
Since $2 < 7.5$, $2$ is an outlier.

questions.question_text:
A dataset of runner times has $Q_1 = 44\text{ s}, Q_3 = 56\text{ s}$, with minimum $30\text{ s}$ and maximum $70\text{ s}$.
Are there any outliers?

options.text: No, all data values lie within the fences of $26\text{ s}$ and $74\text{ s}$.

options.why: Subtracted $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ from $56$ instead of adding to find the upper fence.
Calculated the lower fence as $32\text{ s}$ by using $1 \times \text{IQR}$ instead of $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$.

options.text: Yes, both $30\text{ s}$ and $70\text{ s}$ are outliers.
options.why: Assumed the minimum and maximum must always be outliers without checking fences.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{IQR} = 56 - 44 = 12$
$\text{Lower fence} = 44 - 1.5 \times 12 = 26\text{ s}$
$\text{Upper fence} = 56 + 1.5 \times 12 = 74\text{ s}$
Since $\text{Min} = 30 \ge 26$ and $\text{Max} = 70 \le 74$, there are no outliers.

questions.question_text:
A dataset has a lower quartile of $Q_1 = 14$ and an upper quartile of $Q_3 = 26$.
What is the maximum possible range of this dataset if it contains no outliers?

options.why: Reported the IQR ($26 - 14 = 12$) rather than the maximum possible range.
Quoted the upper fence ($44$) instead of calculating the difference between the upper and lower fences.
Calculated the difference between the upper fence and $Q_1$ ($44 - 14 = 30$) rather than subtracting the lower fence.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{IQR} = 26 - 14 = 12$
$\text{Lower fence} = 14 - 1.5 \times 12 = -4$
$\text{Upper fence} = 26 + 1.5 \times 12 = 44$
$\text{Max possible range} = \text{Upper fence} - \text{Lower fence}$
$= 44 - (-4)$
$= 48$

questions.question_text:
Seven employees earn weekly wages of $\$350, \$500, \$540, \$610, \$690, \$720, \$1080$.
Is the wage of $\$1080$ an outlier using the formal $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule?

options.text: Yes, because $\$1080$ exceeds the upper fence of $\$1050$.
Yes, because $\$1080$ exceeds the upper fence of $\$940$.
options.why: Used $1 \times \text{IQR}$ instead of $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$, calculating $720 + 220 = 940$.

options.text: No, because the upper fence is $\$1470$.
options.why: Used $Q_1 = 500$ instead of the IQR of $220$, calculating $720 + 1.5 \times 500 = 1470$.

options.text: No, because an outlier must exceed $\$1380$.
options.why: Added another $1.5 \times \text{IQR} = 330$ to the correct upper fence, calculating $1050 + 330 = 1380$.
